# Harbour registry

A [Harbour](https://github.com/aryamurray/harbour) registry: a git repository holding real C and C++
packages as **pins and patches** (no upstream source is vendored). It is built to be maintained by
machines as well as by people, so everything a package is, and everything a package is judged by, is a
plain file in this repository, and the index Harbour reads is rendered from those files and checked.

## Use it

In Harbour's global config (`~/.harbour/config.toml`; a non-empty `registries` list REPLACES the
built-in registries, so keep those after it):

```toml
[[registries]]
name = "personal"
url = "https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>"   # or ssh://git@github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git
priority = -10                              # lower wins
```

Harbour fetches with your system `git`, so a private repo works with whatever your git is already set up
for (credential helper, `gh auth setup-git`, ssh keys). Then `harbour add zlib`.

## How it is organised

`packages/` is the **source of truth**. `index/` is **rendered** from it and committed, because Harbour
reads the git repository's `index/` directly (`harbour registry index` is how that tree is produced; there
is no server). `tools/render.py --check` fails CI if `index/` is not exactly what `packages/` produces.

```
packages/<name>/
  package.toml     identity, upstream, releases, test contract
  Harbour.toml     the manifest Harbour builds the package with (what the patch adds)
  overlay/         optional: extra files added to the upstream tree (vendored config header, generator scripts)
  patches/         optional: real fixes to upstream files, as *.patch
  test/            the consumer test: Harbour.toml + src/..., or run.sh for packages needing a custom driver
index/             rendered; never edited by hand
  <l>/<name>.idx                  tier-1 index: one JSON line per version (deps, checksum, license, shim path)
  <l>/<name>/<version>.toml       tier-2 shim: the source pin (tarball url + sha256 + strip_prefix, or git rev) and its patches
  <l>/<name>/<version>.patch      git patch that ADDS Harbour.toml and the overlay files to the upstream tree
  <l>/<name>/<version>-<fix>.patch   one per patches/*.patch, applied first
tools/             render, lint, test, plan, guard (Python 3.11+ standard library only)
.github/           CI, and the action that installs the pinned Harbour
.harbour-version   the harbour commit CI builds and tests against
CODEOWNERS         the judge (tools/, .github/, packages/*/test/, .harbour-version) belongs to a human
```

A simple package and a complex one:

```
packages/zlib/                          packages/cpython/
  package.toml                            package.toml
  Harbour.toml                            Harbour.toml
  test/                                   overlay/harbour/{config.sh,freeze1.sh,freeze2.sh,pyconfig.sh,empty.c}
    Harbour.toml                          overlay/harbour/pyconfig/{linux-aarch64,linux-x86_64,macos-aarch64}.h
    src/main.c                            test/{run.sh,expected-frozen.sha256,consumer/}
```

### `package.toml`

`packages/_template/package.toml` is the annotated reference. In short:

| table | keys |
| --- | --- |
| `[package]` | `name` (= directory), `description`, `license` (SPDX, the upstream's), `homepage` |
| `[upstream]` | `git` (where tags are listed; the clone url for `rev` releases), `tag` (template), `url` (tarball template), `strip_prefix` (template), `scheme` |
| `[[release]]` | `version` (semver), exactly one of `sha256` (tarball) or `rev` (git commit), optional `upstream_version`, `url`, `strip_prefix`, `republish` |
| `[test]` | `platforms` (`linux`/`macos`/`windows`), `objects` (exact translation-unit count: an integer, or `{ default = N, linux = N, "linux-x86_64" = N }`), optional `needs`, `timeout`, `verify` |
| `[review]` | `generators = true`, required when the build runs code (see below) |

Templates expand `{version}` (upstream's spelling), `{major}`, `{minor}`, `{patch}` (from the semver) and,
in `url`/`strip_prefix`, `{tag}`. Unknown keys and placeholders are errors.

### Several versions of one package

`Harbour.toml` and `overlay/` describe **the newest release** (the highest semver in `[[release]]`). The
index is **append-only for older versions**:

* `render.py` rewrites only the newest release's shim and patches. Older releases stay listed in
  `package.toml` (it is the history) and their rendered files stay in `index/` exactly as published; the
  tool only *checks* them (shim present, the pinned sha256/rev matches `package.toml`, each patch hashes to
  what its shim lists) and carries their `.idx` record over.
* A release with no rendered files that is not the newest is an error: nothing keeps an old release's
  manifest, so it cannot be rendered later. Add releases newest-first, one at a time.
* `render.py --check --base <ref>` (what the PR workflow runs) additionally fails if any shim or patch that
  exists at `<ref>` differs now: a published version is immutable, because users' lockfiles pin the patch's
  sha256. Rewriting one on purpose (say, to fix a manifest) is a human decision recorded as
  `republish = "<reason>"` on that `[[release]]`, which stays visible in review; the automated-PR guard
  refuses it for bots outright.

### Versions that are not semver

Harbour requires semver. `version` is always semver; when upstream's spelling differs, put it in
`upstream_version`, and `{version}` in templates then expands to that. `lint.py` checks
`normalize(upstream_version) == version`, so the mapping is reproducible (`render.py --normalize-version X`
prints it):

| upstream | `version` |
| --- | --- |
| `2024-12-28` (date) | `2024.12.28` (leading zeros dropped) |
| `2.10`, `7` | `2.10.0`, `7.0.0` |
| `3.0.0-rc1`, `3.0rc2` | `3.0.0-rc.1`, `3.0.0-rc.2` |
| `1.6.2.1` (four parts) | `1.6.2001`, only with `[upstream] scheme = "four-part"` |

The four-part rule folds the last component into the patch (`A.B.(C*1000+D)`, `D < 1000`) because
build metadata (`1.6.2+1`) is ignored by semver ordering, so `1.6.2.1` and `1.6.2` would tie. It applies to
every release of a package that declares the scheme (`1.6.3` becomes `1.6.3000`), never to some. Any other
shape is refused until `normalize_version()` in `tools/regtools.py` is extended on purpose.

## Add a package

1. `cp -r packages/_template packages/<name>` and replace every `example`.
2. **`package.toml`**: name, description, the upstream's SPDX `license`, `[upstream]` templates, one
   `[[release]]` with its `sha256` (of the exact tarball: `curl -fsSL <url> | sha256sum`) or a git `rev`.
3. **`Harbour.toml`**: the manifest. Name every source file (a source list that silently shrinks still
   links). `[package] version` and `license` must equal the newest release's. Dependencies are other packages
   in this registry, by version.
4. **`test/`**: a consumer that depends on the package *through the registry* and asserts real behaviour,
   printing `OK ...` as its last line. Start from `packages/_template/test` or a sibling package's.
5. `python3 tools/render.py` to render `index/` (and the README table), then `python3 tools/lint.py`.
6. `python3 tools/test.py <name>` with a `harbour` on `PATH` (or `--harbour BIN`). Set `[test] objects` to the
   count it reports, after checking the number is what the library should compile.
7. Commit `packages/<name>/` and the rendered `index/`, open a PR. CI re-checks all of it on every
   platform you listed.

## Bump a version by hand

1. Add a new `[[release]]` above the old one in `package.toml` (`version`, `sha256` or `rev`). Keep the old entry.
2. Set `[package] version` in `Harbour.toml` to the new version; fix the manifest and `overlay/` if the new
   release needs it (new source files, a regenerated vendored header).
3. `python3 tools/render.py && python3 tools/lint.py && python3 tools/test.py <name>`.
4. If the test fails because the library changed (a different source count, a renamed symbol) fix
   `Harbour.toml`; if `[test] objects` is now legitimately different, update it: that is a human edit.
   The old version's rendered files must show no diff.

## The quality bar

A package is in the registry when, on every platform in its `[test] platforms`:

* its **license** is an SPDX expression on the allowlist (`tools/lint.py`; `LicenseRef-*` is allowed for
  licenses SPDX has no identifier for), and it equals the `Harbour.toml` license;
* its source is **pinned by hash** (tarball `sha256`, or full git `rev`) over https;
* it **builds** through the registry with every source pattern matching a file (`--strict-sources`), a second build recompiles nothing, and the consumer **runs and prints `OK`
  as its last line** after asserting real behaviour (round trips, known answers, a server answering commands),
  including that the library reports the version `package.toml` declares;
* it compiles **exactly `[test] objects` translation units**, because a source list that silently shrinks still
  links and still passes.

Code that runs during the build (`prebuild`/`postbuild`/`recipe`, `host = true` targets, scripts in `overlay/`,
patches that add scripts) is allowed only with `[review] generators = true`, so a human sees the flag flip.
`lint.py` also refuses non-https URLs, credentials and secret-looking strings anywhere in a package, symlinks,
CRLF or binary overlay files, and a `[test] platforms` entry the manifest's `supports` excludes.

## The tools

All are Python 3.11+, standard library only, and run on Linux, macOS and Windows (Git Bash).

| tool | what |
| --- | --- |
| `tools/render.py [pkg...]` | render `packages/` into `index/` and the README table. `--check` fails (with a diff) if stale; `--check --base REF` also enforces append-only; `--harbour BIN` lets `harbour registry index` produce/verify the `.idx` files (downloads every package's source) |
| `tools/lint.py [pkg...]` | static checks, no network |
| `tools/test.py pkg... \| --all` | the consumer test, through the registry (below) |
| `tools/plan.py --base REF \| --all` | affected packages (changed + reverse dependencies from the `.idx` files; everything if `tools/`, `.github/`, `.harbour-version` etc. changed) and the CI matrix |
| `tools/guard.py` | the automated-PR guard |
| `tools/rot_issues.py` | the nightly workflow's issue bookkeeping |
| `python3 -m unittest discover -s tools -p "test_*.py"` | tests of the tools (the patch renderer against real `git diff`, the guard against real git history, lint and render against mutated copies of this checkout) |

### Rendering is byte-exact

A shim lists each patch with the sha256 of its exact bytes. `render.py` writes the text `git diff --binary`
prints for the added files (verified against git in the tests), the shim in the generator's format, and the
`.idx` lines in `serde_json`'s compact form. `.gitattributes` carries `*.patch -text` so line-ending
conversion cannot change a patch (`harbour registry index` insists on it). The built-in `.idx` renderer
ports what `harbour registry index` does for registry-only dependencies; CI's `Index` job runs the real
command over everything and fails if the two ever disagree.

### How `tools/test.py` works

It snapshots this checkout's `index/` into a throw-away git repository (Harbour clones registries with git, so
`file://<checkout>` would only see committed files), writes an isolated `HOME` whose
`~/.harbour/config.toml` has that snapshot as the **only** `[[registries]]` entry, copies `test/` to a scratch
directory, and runs `harbour build --strict-sources` (fetch, verify, patch, compile as a dependency) twice, then the consumer.
`--strict-sources` makes every pattern in `sources` and in each active `when` block match a file, so a pattern that
matches nothing is an error rather than a library that quietly shrank; a pattern that is legitimately empty on one
platform belongs in a `when` block for the platforms where it matches.
It requires exit 0, last non-empty line `OK` or `OK ...`, and the dependency's object count (excluding
probes and host tools) to equal `[test] objects` for the platform (`<os>-<arch>`, then `<os>`, then `default`).
The consumer reads `REGISTRY_TEST_UPSTREAM_VERSION` and must check the library reports it.
A package not listing the current platform is skipped with a message. On failure the full log is printed.
(Windows cannot isolate `HOME`: Harbour asks the OS, not the environment, for the home directory, so there the
registry is selected with Harbour's `HARBOUR_TEST_REGISTRY_URL`.)

**`[test] verify = true`** adds a second, independent signal: `harbour verify <pkg> --registry-path <snapshot>
--format json --strict-sources`. It builds the newest release the way a consumer does, includes every public header
that compiles on its own, links a harness against the library (referencing one of its symbols) and runs it, and the
test fails if any stage fails; the harness level that ran is printed. It catches what a hand-written consumer does
not: a header that cannot be included, or a system library missing from the public link surface (it is how libpng's
missing `m` shows up without any consumer touching `pow`). It is opt-in because it is a second release-profile build,
roughly as long again as the test itself (about a minute for harfbuzz, which therefore leaves it off). The harness
is in the library's language, so for a C++ library it is C++ and says nothing about C consumers.

**`test/run.sh`** is the escape hatch for packages that are programs, not libraries (redis, cpython). It runs under
bash with cwd = a scratch directory and the same isolated registry. Environment: `HARBOUR`,
`REGISTRY_TEST_PACKAGE`, `REGISTRY_TEST_VERSION`, `REGISTRY_TEST_UPSTREAM_VERSION`, `REGISTRY_TEST_OBJECTS`,
`REGISTRY_TEST_PLATFORM`, `REGISTRY_TEST_DIR` (the package's `test/`), `REGISTRY_TEST_WORK`,
`REGISTRY_TEST_PYTHON`. It must build the package through the registry inside a project under
`REGISTRY_TEST_WORK` (a stub project depending on it: Harbour builds *every* target of a dependency, programs
included, under `.harbour/target/<profile>/deps/<name>-<version>/`), exercise it, exit 0 and print `OK ...` last.
The runner then applies the same last-line and object-count checks.

## CI

* **`pr.yml`** (`pull_request` only, read-only token, never `pull_request_target`): `guard` (automated PRs),
  `plan` (tool self-tests, lint, `render.py --check --base`, affected set and matrix), `harbour` (build and cache
  Harbour per runner image), `index` (the authoritative `harbour registry index` check), `test` (one leg per
  affected package and platform), and **`PR result`**, the one check to require in branch protection.
* **`nightly.yml`** (weekly and manual): every package on every platform; a failure opens or comments on ONE
  `rot` issue per package, and the issue closes when the package passes again.
* Harbour comes from `.harbour-version` (a commit SHA), built with `cargo build --release --locked` and cached per
  SHA/OS/arch by `.github/actions/setup-harbour`. When Harbour has releases, only that action changes.

### The bot-PR guard

This is the safety property of the autonomous loop the registry is built for: **the judge cannot be modified by
the judged.** A PR is automated if its author login ends in `[bot]`, its user type is Bot, or it carries the
`bot` label. An automated PR may change only `packages/*/package.toml`, `packages/*/Harbour.toml`,
`packages/*/overlay/**`, `packages/*/patches/**` and `index/**` (plus the generated README table). It may not
touch `packages/*/test/**`, `tools/**`, `.github/**`, `.harbour-version` or `CODEOWNERS`; may not change a
`package.toml`'s `[test]`, `[review]`, `name` or `license`; may not add a package; and may only *add* version
files under `index/` (a published version is immutable). `tools/guard.py` implements it and is tested against real
git history.

What makes it hold, beyond the job: CODEOWNERS puts `tools/`, `.github/`, `packages/*/test/` and
`.harbour-version` under a human, and the repository must enable *Require review from Code Owners*, require
the `PR result` check, and keep the bot account out of the bypass list. A `pull_request` workflow runs the
PR's own copy of itself, so a PR that deletes the guard job is only stopped by that branch protection; the
guard's script is therefore fetched from the base commit.

## Not built yet

* **The upstream release detector.** It will read each package's `[upstream] git`/`tag`, find a tag newer than
  the newest `[[release]]`, and open a PR that changes only `package.toml` (a new `[[release]]` with the hash),
  the `Harbour.toml` `version`, and the re-rendered `index/`. The guard already allows exactly that.
* **The repair step.** When a bump no longer builds, an LLM may rewrite `Harbour.toml` / `overlay/` / `patches/`
  in the same PR, using the failing `tools/test.py` log. It may not touch `test/`, `[test]`, `tools/` or
  `.github/`: CI is the merge gate and the guard makes that structural, not a convention.
* Binary overlay files and `.idx` yanking are not supported by the tools yet.
